glance: Local restaurants in Bogura town around Satmatha and Nator Road; best of all at a village gathering if you are invited
bogura-aloo-ghati.desc: Boiled potatoes are broken by hand and cooked into beef that has been simmered with onion, ginger-garlic and whole spices, until the two blend into a thick, spoonable curry. A final tempering of panch phoron, green chilli and fried garlic gives it its smell. Elsewhere ghati is made with fish or egg, but in Bogura it usually means beef. It is the dish of milad and kulkhani gatherings, waz mahfil feasts and picnics, and a classic way to use Eid-ul-Adha meat.

glance: 195 km to Bogura by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
kherua-mosque.desc: Built in 1582 according to its inscription, the Kherua Mosque is one of the earliest surviving mosques from the start of Mughal rule in Bengal. Its thick brick walls, curved cornice and three domes show the local Sultanate style blending with new Mughal ideas. The compound is lawned and peaceful, with tall trees around it. It is an easy detour on the way to or from Bogura.
blocks: How to get there
In Sherpur upazila, about 20 km south of Bogura town on the Dhaka highway; take a rickshaw from Sherpur town.
Good to know
Still used for prayers, so dress modestly and visit outside prayer times.

gokul-medh.desc: South of Mahasthangarh, this ancient brick structure rises from the fields in a honeycomb of walled cells and terraces. Archaeologists date it to around the 6th–7th centuries and see it as a temple or stupa platform. Local tradition calls it the bridal chamber of Behula and Lakhindar from the Manasa legend, where Lakhindar was bitten by a snake despite every precaution. Climbing to the top gives wide views over the green countryside.
blocks: How to get there
A short rickshaw or CNG ride from Mahasthan bazar.
Good to know
Combine with Mahasthangarh on the same day. The steps can be uneven.

govinda-bhita.desc: Govinda Bhita lies on a bend of the Karatoya just north of the Mahasthan citadel, outside the old ramparts. It was first excavated in 1928–29, and the work exposed brick foundations of temple buildings from different periods. Most visitors stop at the main citadel and the museum and never walk the short distance here. The low walls by the river are quiet, and it is a good place to imagine the ancient city of Pundranagar spreading along the water.
blocks: How to get there
From Mahasthan bazar walk or take a rickshaw towards the Mahasthan museum; Govinda Bhita is right beside it.
Good to know
Combine it with Mahasthangarh and the museum on the same trip. There is little shade, so carry water.

bogura-nawab-palace-museum.desc: The Nawab Palace stands on the west bank of the Karatoya in the middle of Bogura town. It belonged to the Nawab family of Bogura, whose best-known member, Mohammad Ali Bogra, became Prime Minister of Pakistan. Since 1998 the two-storey house has been a museum: artist Aminul Karim Dulal filled its rooms with sculptures showing the household at work and leisure, from the billiard room to a music gathering. Outside is a small amusement park with rides for children. The Department of Archaeology declared the palace a protected antiquity in 2016.
blocks: How to get there
It is on Nawab Bari Road near Satmatha in the town centre; walk or take a rickshaw.
Good to know
Open daily from about 10 am to 8 pm. Go in the late afternoon and walk to the Karatoya bank afterwards.

glance: 195 km to Bogura by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
poradaha-mela.desc: Held for one day each winter in Gabtali upazila, Poradaha Mela is best known for its enormous fish, such as boal and other big river and pond fish, brought in for sale. Families invite sons-in-law and relatives, and buying the biggest fish is a point of pride. Alongside the fish market there are sweets, toys, furniture and household goods. It is one of the most talked-about rural fairs in North Bengal.
blocks: How to get there
Take a CNG from Bogura town towards Gabtali and ask for the fair ground; the roads are crowded on the day.
Good to know
Check the date locally, as it follows the Bangla calendar. Arrive early to see the biggest fish before they sell.

bogura-doi.desc: Bogura's sweet doi is made by slowly reducing milk with sugar until it turns creamy and lightly browned, then setting it in unglazed clay pots. The pot draws out moisture, leaving a dense yogurt you can almost cut with a spoon. Its roots are traced to Sherpur in the south of the district, and today countless sweet shops in Bogura town make their own versions. It is served at weddings and family meals across the country.
blocks: Good to know
Buy a sealed clay pot to carry home; it keeps for a day or two without refrigeration in cool weather.

Sweet shops and grocers across Bogura town; the factories cluster in Bejora, Chelopara and Naruli
bogura-laccha-semai.desc: Laccha semai is wheat dough worked with fat, pulled into fine layered strands and fried into crisp, flaky nests. Bogura is the biggest maker in the country: hundreds of small factories in town neighbourhoods such as Bejora, Chelopara and Naruli, and along the Karatoya, run day and night before Eid. At home it is simmered briefly in sweetened milk, or just warmed with sugar and ghee. Ghee-fried batches are the premium kind.
blocks: Good to know
The weeks before Eid are when production peaks and the choice is widest.

vasu-bihar.desc: In the countryside north-west of Mahasthangarh lie the brick foundations of Buddhist monasteries and a temple, excavated in the 1970s. The layout of cells around courtyards is still clear, and the site is thought to be linked with the monastic centre described by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang. There are no crowds, just fields, birdsong and old brick. It gives a sense of how large the Buddhist presence around Pundranagar once was.
blocks: How to get there
Hire a CNG or auto-rickshaw from Mahasthan bazar; the road passes through villages in Shibganj upazila.
Good to know
There are few facilities, so carry water. Ask your driver to wait for the return trip.

mahasthangarh.desc: Mahasthangarh is a raised, rectangular citadel beside the Karatoya River, enclosed by brick ramparts that still run for several kilometres. Excavations have revealed layers from the Maurya period through the Gupta, Pala and later eras, making it one of the oldest known urban sites in Bengal. You can walk along the walls, see temple and monastery foundations, and visit the site museum nearby. The shrine of Shah Sultan Balkhi Mahisawar on the mound draws a steady stream of pilgrims.
blocks: How to get there
About 13 km north of Bogura town on the Bogura–Rangpur highway; buses and CNGs stop at Mahasthan bazar.
Good to know
Wear good shoes for walking the ramparts and carry water. The museum has a weekly closing day.

mahasthan-kotkoti.desc: Kotkoti are small fried pieces of dough coated in jaggery or sugar syrup, crisp on the outside and slightly chewy within. Stalls lining the road at Mahasthan sell them in large heaps, and pilgrims to the shrine traditionally take a packet home. They are simple and very sweet, best eaten fresh. Watching the sellers weigh out paper bags is part of the visit.
blocks: Good to know
Ask to taste before buying, as quality varies between stalls.

glance: 195 km to Bogura by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
sariakandi-jamuna-ghat.desc: Sariakandi upazila sits on the right bank of the Jamuna, and much of it is water and shifting sandbank. To protect the bank, long groynes were built at Kalitola and nearby places, and these have become spots where people come to walk, sit by the river and watch the sunset. From the ghats, boats take visitors out to the chars to see village life on the river islands. In the monsoon the river is huge and fast; in winter it shrinks and the sandbars stand out.
blocks: How to get there
Sariakandi is about 22 km east of Bogura town; take a CNG or bus, then a rickshaw to Kalitola ghat.
Good to know
Agree the boat fare before you set off and wear a life jacket. Avoid boat trips in bad weather or when the river is rising.

glance: Markets in Sariakandi upazila town and the Jamuna char villages, in the dry season
sariakandi-red-chilli.desc: The sandy chars of the Jamuna in Sariakandi, Sonatala and Dhunat grow much of Bogura's chilli crop, and agriculture officials rate the Sariakandi char chilli among the best in the country. In the dry season the chars turn red as the ripe chillies are picked and spread out to dry, with hundreds of women sorting them by hand. Dried, they go into the hot red pastes and bhortas of North Bengal cooking. Buying a bag here is a cheap, very local souvenir.
